cards.design_implication: If high thermal anisotropy is required, one could design materials using van der Waals thin films with random interlayer rotations to decouple in-plane and through-plane thermal conductivity.
does_not_establish: Generalizability to all van der Waals materials.
Performance metrics for devices other than simple heat spreaders/electrodes.
cards.evidence_excerpt: Here we report extremely anisotropic thermal conductors based on large-area van der Waals thin flms with random interlayer rotations, which produce a room-temperature thermal anisotropy ratio close to 900 in MoS , one of the highest ever reported. This is enabled by the interlayer rotations that impede the through-plane thermal transport, while the long-range intralayer crystallinity maintains high in-plane thermal conductivity.
limitations: Applies specifically to MoS2 films with random interlayer rotations.
Observation is limited to room temperature conditions.
cards.statement: In random stacked TMD films, interlayer rotation impedes through-plane thermal transport while maintaining in-plane crystallinity, leading to a room-temperature thermal anisotropy ratio of approximately 900.

cards.design_implication: To replicate through-plane thermal conductivity measurements in similar anisotropic films, calibrate TDTR instruments to use a 785 nm laser at 74.86 MHz and ensure minimal heating (<4 K rise) to avoid non-linear effects.
does_not_establish: Alternative methods for measuring thermal conductivity.
Suitability of these settings for materials with significantly different thermal properties.
cards.evidence_excerpt: We used a mode-locked Ti:sapphire laser, which produced a train of pulses at a repetition rate of 74.86 MHz, with wavelength centred at 785 nm and a total power of 18 mW. The steady-state temperature rise at the surface of the samples was <4 K for all temperatures.
limitations: Specific to the experimental setup described for this study.
cards.statement: Time domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) was used to measure through-plane thermal conductivity, requiring a laser system with a 785 nm wavelength, 74.86 MHz repetition rate, and 18 mW total power, while maintaining a steady-state temperature rise of less than 4 K.
